title: India Gets Blood Test to Detect Hidden Cancer Recurrence After Treatment
excerpt: MedGenome has launched OncoTrack MRD, described as India's first indigenous blood test that can detect residual cancer at the molecular level even when scans show no visible disease.
body:
• MedGenome has launched OncoTrack MRD, a blood test that detects residual cancer by tracking circulating tumour DNA, even when conventional scans show no visible disease.
  • The test creates a personalised molecular profile from each patient's own tumour tissue and can be repeated multiple times a year through standard blood draws.
  • It covers major solid tumours including breast, lung, colorectal, ovarian and pancreatic cancers.
  • India diagnoses an estimated 1.5 million new cancer cases each year, and early detection of recurrence remains a major challenge.

A Test That Looks Beyond Scans

Bengaluru-based genomics company MedGenome has launched OncoTrack MRD, described as India's first indigenous, personalised blood test for detecting residual cancer after treatment. The Next-Generation Sequencing-based test was launched in Bengaluru on September 3, according to Express Healthcare.

The core idea is straightforward: a cancer scan can show doctors what is visible, but microscopic disease can persist undetected until it progresses into a full recurrence. OncoTrack MRD addresses that gap by tracking circulating tumour DNA in the bloodstream at a molecular level.

The test works by first creating a customised molecular profile using a patient's own tumour tissue and a baseline blood sample. Once this personalised profile is established, subsequent monitoring can be carried out through a standard blood draw, enabling oncologists to assess the risk of recurrence earlier than conventional imaging alone.

How It Works

Unlike generic cancer screening panels, OncoTrack MRD uses tumour-informed testing — meaning it identifies signals specific to each patient's own tumour rather than relying on a fixed set of mutations. The company says this allows the test to track tumour-specific circulating tumour DNA with greater sensitivity.

The test can be applied across a broad range of solid tumours, including breast, colorectal, lung, ovarian and other gynaecological cancers, as well as pancreatic, oesophageal, gastric, hepatocellular and thoracic cancers and melanoma. MedGenome particularly highlights its use for resected Stage II/III colorectal cancer, early-stage non-small cell lung cancer and early or locally advanced breast cancer after curative-intent treatment.

"While imaging remains an essential part of cancer follow-up, microscopic disease can sometimes remain undetected until it progresses. Tumour-informed MRD testing offers clinicians a powerful tool to identify patients who may require closer surveillance or timely intervention."

— Dr. Niti Raizada, Principal Director of Medical Oncology, Fortis Hospitals

India's Cancer Burden

With India diagnosing an estimated 1.5 million new cancer cases every year, early detection of recurrence is one of the most significant challenges in cancer care, according to City Today News. Many patients may be at risk of cancer returning even when there are no visible signs through conventional clinical assessment or imaging.

Dr. Vedam Ramprasad, CEO of MedGenome Labs, said the growing cancer burden has increased the need for more precise monitoring tools. "Our personalised and ultra-sensitive NGS-based tumour-informed MRD test adds an important layer of molecular insight to complement existing clinical assessment and imaging," he said.

The company has started an academic MRD study and is encouraging oncologists and hospitals to participate, with patients in the study not being charged, according to Express Healthcare.

The Evidence So Far

MedGenome points to global clinical evidence from the GALAXY study, part of the CIRCULATE-Japan programme, as well as the IMvigor011 and ADAURA trials to support the role of tumour-informed ctDNA monitoring. However, clinicians at the launch event noted that the evidence around MRD-guided treatment is still developing across different tumour types, and a positive MRD result does not automatically dictate the same treatment decision across all solid cancers.

The test is designed to complement, rather than replace, imaging and clinical assessment. Dr. Vinayak Maka of Ramaiah Memorial Hospital said, "The future of cancer care is not just about treating the disease we can see, but also detecting and monitoring the disease we cannot yet see."

Broader Reach

MedGenome says genomic testing is moving beyond India's biggest cities. According to Dr. Ramprasad, 27% of the company's samples now come from Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities, a significant shift from seven years ago. The company offers more than 1,300 genetic tests across oncology, inherited diseases, reproductive health and preventive wellness, and has sequenced more than 600,000 exomes and genomes across a network of 8,000 hospitals and 27,000 clinicians in India. OncoTrack MRD is available with home sample collection and nationwide delivery.
